title: Nutrition Knowledge, Self-Efficacy, Social Support, and Healthy Lifestyle Adoption Among a Female University Population: A Cross-Sectional Study at Jazan University, Saudi Arabia
content: Background: Unhealthy dietary patterns and nutrition literacy level are some of the major modifiable risk factors for non-communicable disease in Saudi Arabia. Theoretically, nutrition knowledge, self-efficacy for healthy eating and perceived social support are believed to play a role in healthy lifestyle adoption, but there is a limited local evidence of these constructs from university samples in the Jazan region. Design: A descriptive study.Objective: To describe the nutrition knowledge, self-efficacy and perceived social support of female students and staff of Jazan University and to investigate their relationships with self-reported Body Mass Index (BMI). Methods: A cross-sectional design was used. The researcher gathered the data using a self-administered online questionnaire, filled out in Arabic and English, which included the following items: sociodemographic items, eight multiple-choice items on nutrition knowledge, a seven-item self-efficacy scale and a six-item perceived social support scale (both on 5-point Likert scales) and self-reported height and weight. Internal consistency was measured for the Likert scales with Cronbach’s alpha and for the knowledge items with KR-20. Spearman correlation coefficient, Kruskal-Wallis test and multiple linear regression were used to look at associations. A p-value of < 0.05 was defined as statistically significant. Twenty-four people filled out the survey (75.0% students, 20.8% faculty, 4.2% administrative/technical staff; 62.5% age 18-22 years). The mean score for nutrition knowledge was 6.58/8 (SD = 1.59; 82.3% correct) with the lowest mean item correctness rate of 41.7% on the recommended daily fruit/vegetable servings item. Mean self-efficacy was 3.39 (SD = 0.65, range 1-5) and mean perceived social support was 3.36 (SD = 0.57). The reliability of the self-efficacy scale was acceptable (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.70), as was that of the knowledge scale (KR-20 = 0.64), but not for the social support scale (alpha = 0.54). After two underweight/height and overweight/height pairs were excluded, the average self-reported BMI of the remaining 22 cases was 23.9 kg/m2 (SD = 5.2) and 29.2% of the subjects were classified as underweight and 20.8% were considered obese. There was a significant (Spearman’s rho = -0.47, p = 0.026) and negative correlation between BMI and perceived social support in a multiple regression model controlling for nutrition knowledge (B = -6.89, p = 0.009). The role and age group were not significantly related to knowledge or self-efficacy or to social support (p > 0.05 for all). Conclusion: This preliminary sample showed that nutrition knowledge was relatively high, but varied by topic. Self-reported BMI was most closely related to perceived social support, and not to nutrition knowledge. Although these preliminary findings from a small convenience sample should be interpreted with caution and future studies with a larger, more adequately powered sample are needed to confirm these results, the results do suggest that social-support oriented components would be a potentially useful addition to campus nutrition education programming.
